mes:
*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

`SYSTEM INITIALIZATION COMPLETE`
`Origin: Earth`
`World: Avereth`
`Race: Human`
`Age: 18`
`Level: 1 | Rank: F`

`BASE STATS`
`STR 5 | VIT 5 | AGI 5 | INT 5 | PER 5 | WIL 5`

`Location: Public roadside verge outside Glassmere, Caelreth`
`Arrival Witnesses: NONE`
`Starting Possessions: Simple Traveler's Clothes | Small Pouch | 5 Silver`
`Local Common Language: Integrated`
`Mandatory Quest: NONE`

`CHARACTER CREATION — STEP 1/2`
`Choose your Base Class:`

`Warrior   — Favored Stats: STR / VIT`
`Mage      — Favored Stats: INT / WIL`
`Rogue   — Favored Stats: AGI / PER`

`Your chosen Class immediately applies +1 to both Favored Stats at Level 1.`
`After choosing a Class, select exactly 2 Skills from that Class's Base Skill Pool.`

`Reply with your Class choice.`

*The System waits. Story time does not move during Character Creation.*

mes:
The road took him at its own pace. Cart ruts ran hard and dry between the verge and the fields, and ahead the walls of Glassmere grew out of the morning haze in slow stages — first a gray smear, then the pale line of the rampart, then the towers over the gate, each one flying a banner that snapped and settled in the wind. Traffic thickened as he walked: a drover with six sheep, a woman leading a mule stacked with firewood, two men on foot who nodded to him the way country people nod to anyone on a road.

The gate stood open. A queue of maybe a dozen moved through without hurry, and the guards there barely looked up — one glance at his sword, another at his face, nothing more. No toll was asked of a man arriving on foot with nothing to sell. The passage through the wall smelled of cold stone and old torch smoke, and then the city opened in front of him.

Morning noise everywhere: shutters being folded back, a smith's hammer somewhere to the left, bread-smell drifting from an oven house, water running in an open gutter down the middle of the street. The crowd was thick enough to shoulder through but not press against him. Caelreth's learning showed in small ways — a painted sign advertising enchanted lamp-oil, a boy hurrying past with a satchel of books, a shop window displaying Skill-Stones on velvet behind wire.

He asked nothing. He didn't need to. Two streets in, a carved board hung from an iron bracket above a wide arched doorway: a crossed sword and lantern beneath the words **Adventurers' Guild — Glassmere Branch**. Through the open doors came lamplight, the murmur of voices, and the clack of wooden practice swords from somewhere deeper in.

A broad-shouldered man in mail stood just inside the entrance, talking with a clerk at a side desk. The front counter sat empty, waiting.

The clerk behind the counter was a thin woman with ink-stained fingers and a stack of contract slips she was squaring against the wood. She set the stack down when he stopped in front of her and looked him over the way the gate guards had — face, sword, then face again.

"Registration." She said it like a word she'd said twice already this morning. "I can do it here. You'll need two silver for the fee, one time only, and that's the whole of it. You sign the roll, we take your measure on the stone, and you leave with a rank and a slip."

She tilted her head toward a block of pale stone sitting at the end of the counter, worn smooth on top from years of hands.

"Stone reads what you are. No arguing with it, no talking your way up or down. Whatever it says is what you are." She pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward her, then paused, quill hovering. "Nobody's turned away for a low reading, if that's what you're wondering. Half this hall started at the bottom. Fee's still two silver either way."

Behind him, the man in mail laughed at something the side-desk clerk had said, and the clack of practice swords came again from the deeper rooms, steady as a heartbeat.

"So." The clerk looked at him, quill still waiting over the page. "Two silver, and your name spelled out for the roll. Do we start?"

The words left him — spoken aloud this time, plain as a market price — and still the interface did not fold. The four names sat in their places, Cleave and Shield Bash, Bull's Stamina and War Cry, the instruction beneath them unchanged: select exactly 2. It was as if he were reading the list out to a stone wall. No warmth, no settling, no sense of anything taking hold.

The clerk's hand was still out, palm up, waiting for his.

"You're doing it again." Her voice dropped a shade, and the woman in oiled leather behind him leaned to see past his shoulder. "Staring through me like I'm a window. If you're feeling faint, say so and sit down, but don't stand at my counter swaying."

She withdrew the hand and folded her arms instead, quill tucked behind one ear, and studied him the way a buyer studies a beast that stands wrong in its harness.

"Here's what I know," she said. "You agreed a fee, you gave a name, and then you stopped halfway through like a man who's forgotten why he walked into a room. I can't register a name the ink won't take, and I can't read a stone you won't touch. So." She tapped the counter twice with one knuckle. "Either put your hand flat on that stone and finish what you started, or step aside and let the woodcutter behind you have his turn. You can come back when you've gathered yourself. The Guild doesn't chase people out — but it doesn't hold places in line either."

The boy with the axe shifted his weight and looked at the floor, embarrassed for everyone.

The prompt hung where it had always hung, and the two skills he had named stayed as unclaimed as coins on the far side of a river.

His palm met the stone and the cold of it climbed into his fingers — colder than a counter-top had any right to be, like a slab kept in a cellar. Then the cold moved. It slid up through the meat of his hand, along the bones of his forearm, and settled across his chest for the space of two heartbeats before draining back down and away.

A faint line of light crossed the stone's surface under his hand, pale gold, running left to right and then fading.

The clerk leaned over to read what it left behind and whistled through her teeth, low.

"There we go. That's the trick of it." She pulled the quill from behind her ear and bent to the ledger. "Strong frame on you, and it says you're holding up well under it. Good bones for the work." The quill scratched, stopped. She looked up. "And the class line. You said it before — I heard you say it — but the ink won't carry it unless you say it to me again, plain, while the reading's still fresh. That's just how the registration works. So: what are you?"

Behind him the woman in oiled leather had stopped trying to see past his shoulder and was simply watching him now, openly. The woodcutter boy had given up on the floor and was looking at him too.

The prompt still hung in his vision, patient as ever, the four skill names waiting in their places. Exactly 2, it said. It had not accepted anything yet — not from his mouth, not from his mind. Whatever door his voice was knocking on, this was not the one.

The clerk dipped her quill and held it over the empty line.

"Whenever you're ready. The stone's warm once, and only once."

"Warrior." The clerk said it back to the ledger rather than to him, and this time the quill ran. The letters came onto the page in a smooth line, ink dark and willing, and she made a small satisfied sound in her throat as if a stubborn horse had finally stepped into its stall.

"There. One name, one class, one reading. That's a registration." She sanded the line, blotted it, and turned the ledger a half-circle so the entry faced him — Alaric, Warrior, the stone's marks copied out beside it in her tidy hand. "Welcome to the Guild, such as it is at your rank. Which is to say: the bottom, same as everyone starts. Don't take it as an insult. I signed my own name on that line eleven years ago and my first job was carrying frog grease for an apothecary."

She held up one finger before he could move.

"Two silver. You agreed to it. Pay and the slip's yours — the contract slip with your name on it, lightly charmed so it knows what job it's tied to and nothing else. Then you're free to read the board."

Behind him the woodcutter boy had crept half a step closer, and the woman in oiled leather muttered something to him — "kept him waiting half the morning, Mam would say" — but not with any real heat in it. Through the open doors the street noise rolled in: a cart's iron-rimmed wheel, a fishmonger crying prices, the smell of wet stone and bread.

Somewhere behind his eyes, the prompt with its four names sat exactly where it had been. The clerk's ledger had taken Warrior from his mouth. That other thing, whatever it was, still wanted something else — and had not said what would work.

The clerk put out her hand for the coin.

"Two silver, and you walk out of here a member."

The two silver crossed the counter with a small double click, and the clerk swept them into a drawer without counting what she could plainly see.

"Pleasure doing business." She pulled a slip of pale parchment from a stack beneath the counter and laid it flat, and her quill moved over it in three short strokes — name, branch, day. The ink settled with a faint shimmer, the charm taking hold, and she turned it and slid it across to him between two fingers. "Alaric. Glassmere branch. That's yours now. Don't lose it — it's what tells another branch you're a member and not some fool who heard about the Guild from a drunk. Wet weather curls them, so keep it dry."

She was already turning the ledger back toward herself, dipping the quill, but she gave him one more look over the top of it.

"Board's on the far wall, left of the hearth. Nothing there this morning when I opened up, but folk pin things up when they pin them up. Worth a walk past." The quill touched parchment. "Next."

The woodcutter boy stepped up so fast he nearly clipped Alaric's elbow with his axe handle, mumbling an apology, and then he was filling the space at the counter and the clerk's attention had moved on with him. "Name's Osper," Alaric heard behind him, "and I need — well, I need whatever's cheapest, mostly."

The hall opened up beyond the counter: long room, scarred tables, a hearth burning low, a notice board of weathered planks by the far wall with one curled paper on it and several bare nails. A woman in oiled leather peeled away from the queue and crossed toward the door, pausing there with a hand on the frame — not looking at him, or looking at him only the way one looks at anyone who has made a morning take longer than it should. Then she pushed out into the street noise and was gone.

The slip sat in Alaric's hand, cool and faintly stiff. The prompt with its four names hung where it had hung all morning, waiting, having taken nothing yet.

mes:
The far wall had planks and nails, all right — but as he crossed the cool flagstones toward it, the clerk's voice came after him over the scratch of her quill.

"Ho — the board's for members, love. You've not signed yet." She was leaning past Osper to see around him, quill still dripping. "You said your piece to the stone and then we got talking about coin and the morning ran off with us. Two silver and your name in the book, and then every nail on that wall is yours to read. Until then it's just wood."

She said it without sharpness — a thing said a dozen times a week, worn smooth — and then went back to Osper, who was explaining that he had three copper and a half and a need for work that didn't involve heights.

The curled paper was too far off to read from here, a pale curl of parchment pinned at the top of the board with its bottom edge hanging loose. Whatever was written on it stayed the board's business.

Behind the counter the clerk's voice ran on. "Three copper and a half doesn't register anyone, Osper, it buys you bread. What it can do is — hold on, there's a standing notice—" drawer noise, paper noise — "here. Rat work in the tannery cellars. Not Guild work, the tanner pays direct, two copper a night and you keep what you catch. That more your weight?"

The hall smelled of woodsmoke and old boot leather. Rain had started somewhere outside; it ticked against the shutters and the street noise softened under it.

The clerk was still holding the notice out to Osper, and the counter stood between Alaric and the board, two silver short.

mes:
The clerk looked up from Osper's three copper and a half, and this time there was nothing to argue about. Two silver crossed the counter and went into the drawer with the same uncounted sweep.

"Well, finally." She pulled the ledger back around, dipped the quill, and wrote without any of the morning's trouble — the letters taking to the page smooth and dark, as if the paper had only been waiting for the coin. *Alaric. Warrior.* She sanded it, blotted it, and turned it for him to see. "There. That's you in the book, and the book doesn't rub out. Eleven years and I still like that part."

A slip came off the stack, three strokes of the quill, the charm settling into the parchment with its faint shimmer, and she slid it across. "Glassmere branch. Keep it dry. Board's yours now — far wall, left of the hearth."

Osper shifted his weight at the counter, tucking the tannery notice into his shirt with one hand and holding his ground with the other. "I was here first, near enough."

"You were here second and you're three copper short of anything," the clerk said, not unkindly. "Let the man read a board. It takes a minute."

The curled paper was close enough now to read. It hung from a nail at the top of the planks, its bottom edge curling with damp, and it was written in a hurried, slanting hand — no Guild stamp, no charm-shimmer in the ink. Just words:

*Wanted — able hand or two, for clearing of fallen stone from a cellar stair off Chandler's Row. Dangerous work, wall's cracked. Four copper the day and bread at noon. Ask for Mistress Harsk at the blue door with the iron ring.*

Beneath it, bare nails. Rain ticked against the shutters. Behind him, Osper was trying again — "but the tanner's two a night, and rats is easy—" — and the clerk's quill scratched on.
